You should review the Air France fatal crash of an A330 in the South Atlantic on June 1, 2009.

The commercial aviation world is complicated by the existence of two sets of human controls and two humans potentially using them. Furthermore, there is a seniority relationship that officially exists (Pilot / Copilot), which can be partially overridden by consent to give equal opportunity for gaining experience (Pilot Flying / Pilot Monitoring). Boeing has taken a leading role in developing the management practice of Crew Resource Management (CRW) that addresses this complex world.

Boeing and Airbus technology also differs in that Boeing physically links the two sets of controls, while Airbus does not! This actually contributed to the Airbus accident, since the senior pilot was off the flight deck resting, and his (left) seat was occupied by the crew with 3rd seniority, while the Pilot Flying was in the right seat. The proximate cause of the crash was conflicting control inputs that neither pilot sensed, and were only detected when the senior captain returned to the flight deck and observed it... too late for a recovery from the dive! Apparently the left controls take priority in conflicts, but the right seat thought he was flying! The senior captain's last recorded words were to the effect that "You two idiots have killed us all!"

As if all this is not bad enough, the whole incident was precipitated by an instrument failure, loss of pitot tube heat, pitot freezing, and consequent loss of airspeed inputs, and finally autopilot disconnection!

These facts have obvious implications for the issue of human-machine interaction!
